# Dukamātikā (Ds 1.2)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dukamātikā* ("Matrix of Dyads") forms the second major division of the mātikā at the head of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, the first book of the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka [Rhys Davids 1900; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. It comprises one hundred twofold classifications (dyads or couplets) of phenomena (*dhamma*), traditionally grouped into clusters or chapters such as the root cluster (*hetugocchaka*), taint cluster (*āsavagocchaka*), fetter cluster (*saññojanagocchaka*), tie cluster (*ganthagocchaka*), and larger intermediate dyads (*mahantaraduka*) [Rhys Davids 1900; Nyanatiloka 1938; Tan Poh Beng 2015; DharmaNexus]. Most of these dyads are formulated as pairs of contradictory or complementary terms, such as phenomena that are roots and those that are not [Watanabe 1983; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The primary hundred dyads are followed by a supplementary section termed the *Suttantadukamātikā*, consisting of forty-two (or forty-six) dyads drawn largely from suttas such as the *Saṅgītisutta*, which the commentary (*Atthasālinī*) attributes to the Elder Sāriputta [Rhys Davids 1900; U Kyaw Khine 1999; Frauwallner 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

Together with the *Tikamātikā*, the *Dukamātikā* serves as the core matrix of the Abhidhamma system [Rhys Davids 1900; U Kyaw Khine 1999]. Its categories are systematically explicated across subsequent books of the Abhidhamma, providing the framework for the *Dukanikkhepa* and *Dukaatthuddhāra* sections of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and forming the combinatory basis for conditional relations in the *Paṭṭhāna* (such as the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* and *Tika-duka-paṭṭhāna*) [Rhys Davids 1900; Payuto; DharmaNexus]. Beyond scholastic analysis, the *Dukamātikā* has held a prominent liturgical role in Southeast Asian Theravāda traditions, where it is ritually chanted in paritta and funerary contexts [Walker].

DharmaNexus identifies over 2,300 text-reuse matches across 80 Pali texts, reflecting massive internal reuse throughout the Abhidhamma, especially in the *Patthāna*, *Vibhaṅga*, and *Abhidhammamātikāpāḷi* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records cross-language alignments with Sanskrit scholastic works (such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* and Vimalamitra's *Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti*) and Tibetan translations of the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* [DharmaNexus], underscoring the ancient and shared heritage of the Abhidharma couplet matrices across early Buddhist traditions [Anderson 1999; Frauwallner 1995].
